item: The session sentinel (session_state.json) is written through the house atomic_replace helper, so two servers on one data folder can no longer tear it or lose a swap
summary: forensics._write_state wrote session_state.json through the one fixed copy name session_state.json.tmp, which every server on a data folder (R176) shared: the second writer truncated the first's open file and the first swap moved that half-written file into place (a mixture of two states in the sentinel the next boot reads), or the second's swap found nothing to move and its state was lost with a warning. Measured on the old writer with two threads standing in for two servers. The writer now calls the house helper file_lock.atomic_replace(..., fsync=False) (the call expedition.py makes): a copy named session_state.json.tmp.<pid>.<thread>, removed if the swap fails, dead processes' copies swept; the last swap wins as before; no sync, as before. The first version hand-rolled the copy, the sweep and a sync; an independent read found defects in it (a stray name that raised, no tolerance for a filesystem without fsync, a sync on the drive-disconnected shutdown path) that the helper already handles, so the hand-rolled code was deleted. 11 tests in tests/test_forensics_state_write.py: 4 fail on the old writer (the half-way writer, the lost swap, a refused swap leaving its copy, the per-thread name), 7 are controls that pass on both (bytes, kill-at-write and kill-at-swap old-sentinel-whole, next write removes a killed process's copy, a copy that cannot be serialised, no-psutil still writes); mutants caught: shared name (4), fsync=True (the not-synced pin), sweep removed from file_lock (the dead-copy removal). The module leaves the unlocked-write allowlist in tests/test_shared_file_writes.py (2 sites to none). Stated: this is the R175 shape, not the R176 conversion (the read-modify-write is not under file_lock); an older-version server still swaps the old fixed name; the helper's sweep judges liveness by bare pid, so a server in another pid namespace on the same folder can lose one in-flight write (reproduced by the independent read on the first version's sweep, which used the same rule; the helper's sweep has it too for an unlocked caller, inferred, not run; house-wide, not changed here; a copy stranded under the process's own pid is skipped as its own, a few hundred bytes).
